title: Executive summary
body: Executive summary Fabric development without source control is a set of unversioned changes made directly to live workspaces by whoever has access. This playbook replaces that with a disciplined engineering practice: every change is versioned, reviewed by a second person, recoverable, and promoted through a controlled path. The mechanics are straightforward. The failure modes are not, and most of this document is about those. What the integration gives you Microsoft Fabric implements application lifecycle management through two complementary mechanisms. Git integration connects a workspace to a repository branch and folder, writing item definitions out as human-readable text so they can be versioned, branched, diffed, reviewed and restored. Deployment pipelines promote content across Development, Test and Production stages, rebinding environment-specific configuration as content moves. Git integration is the continuous-integration half; deployment pipelines are the continuous-delivery half. They are designed to be used together and neither replaces the other. A third mechanism, the Variable Library, holds environment-specific values with a separate value set per stage. It is what allows the same item definition to point at different data in different workspaces. It did not exist in earlier iterations of this pattern and it is the single most useful addition, because it closes the gap described below. The ten conclusions that matter The ten conclusions that matter 1 The first synchronization is the most dangerous action in the whole integration. Connecting a workspace to a non-empty branch folder and choosing Update workspace from Git deletes workspace items. A folder containing nothing but a README still counts as non-empty. Always connect to a genuinely empty folder, then commit a baseline immediately. Section 7 2 Clone before you connect. A Fabric workspace, unlike a Git branch, cannot be rolled back to an earlier state. Use a deployment pipeline stage to clone the workspace as a rollback target, re-hydrate its data, and verify it runs before touching source-control settings. Section 7.2 3 Authentication is two-tier and cannot be collapsed. The workspace-to-GitHub connection is user-delegated and authenticated by an individual's fine-grained personal access token; service principal authentication for the Git connection is documented for Azure DevOps and not for GitHub. Automation uses a separate Entra ID service principal whose credentials live in environment-scoped GitHub secrets. Section 5 4 Branch-out copies items, not data. A branch workspace is an isolated copy of the code and definitions only. A notebook in it still points at the lakehouse it was branched from. Without a Variable Library or automated seeding, a developer can corrupt shared data while believing they are in a sandbox. Section 13 5 Folder structure changes need their own commit. If the workspace has folders that the branch does not, the two are considered different. Updating before committing lets the branch's structure overwrite the workspace's — deleting the new folders and everything in them. Section 7.4 6 Rulesets, not legacy branch protection. Rulesets layer, are visible to anyone with read access, can be enabled and disabled without deletion, and can be applied organization-wide. They also offer rules that map directly onto Fabric's own constraints — file size, path length and path restrictions. Section 16 7 Grant permissions to teams, never to people. Four teams — administrators, reviewers, developers, auditors — mapped to the Admin, Maintain, Write and Read repository roles produce a clean separation of duties. Source team membership from the identity provider so that leavers lose access automatically. Section 15 8 Deployment credentials belong to an environment, not a repository. title: How to use this playbook
body: How to use this playbook Reading paths The document is written to be read end to end once, then used as a reference. If time is short, these are the shortest useful paths through it. Reading paths by role and purpose Standing up the integration for the first time Sections 4, 5, 6, 7, then Appendix C Prerequisites, identity, naming, the safe connection procedure and the runbook checklist. Do not connect a workspace before reading Section 7. A developer joining a team already using this pattern Sections 3, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14 Concepts, how synchronization actually behaves, the branching model, branch workspaces, the data isolation problem and the pull request process. Hardening an environment that already works Sections 15, 16, 17, 18 Access model, rulesets, environments and secrets, optional automated scanning. Responding to a bad change in production Section 19, then Appendix F Rollback decision, the two procedures, re-syncing Fabric, and the command reference. Building a business case or an implementation plan Sections 1, 2, 21, 22 Executive summary, scope, the phased roadmap and the strategic recommendations. Auditing the environment Sections 15, 16, 17, 20, Appendix D Who can do what, what the repository enforces, how credentials are scoped, and what evidence exists. Conventions Typographic and callout conventions <angle brackets> A placeholder to be resolved for your environment. See Section 0.3. Monospace A literal value, command, file name, setting name or identifier. Italic A user-interface element the reader is asked to click or select. → Navigation through a user interface, e.g. Workspace settings → Git integration. CAUTION callout An action that can destroy work. Read before acting. RULE callout A non-negotiable operating rule for the environment. PRACTICE callout A recommended practice with a stated rationale, which a team may reasonably vary. NOTE callout Clarification, platform behaviour or a version caveat. LOCALIZE callout A decision this playbook deliberately leaves to the adopting organization. On preview features A number of capabilities described here — including several item types, branch workspace admin profiles, selective branching and file-level commit — were in preview at the time of writing. Preview behaviour changes without notice and is generally not covered by production support commitments. Verify the current state of anything you intend to depend on, and prefer a design that degrades gracefully if a preview capability is withdrawn. How to adapt rather than copy The temptation with a playbook is to adopt it verbatim. Three decisions genuinely depend on your context and should be made deliberately rather than inherited: Repository granularity. One repository per project is the default recommended here. A single repository for an entire estate simplifies governance but couples release cadences; one repository per workspace fragments review. Section 6.3 sets out the trade-off. Who may create workspaces. Branch-out is far more useful when developers can create their own workspaces. Many organizations restrict workspace creation to a central administration team. Section 12.4 describes the capability that reconciles the two. How much automation to build. Sections 16 and 18 mark automated status checks as optional. The manual gates — required reviews, protected branches, environment approvals — deliver most of the risk reduction. Automated testing of notebooks and data quality is a worthwhile second phase, not a prerequisite.

title: Core concepts
body: Core concepts Three platform mechanisms, one repository model and one branching model account for everything else in this playbook. Understanding what each is responsible for — and, more usefully, what each is not responsible for — prevents most design mistakes. Continuous integration and continuous delivery, in a Fabric context Continuous integration is the practice of merging changes from multiple contributors into a shared branch frequently, with automated verification on each merge. In Fabric terms it means that a notebook, semantic model or pipeline definition is committed to a branch, reviewed by someone other than its author, and integrated into a trunk that is known to be good. Continuous delivery extends this so that an integrated change can be promoted to a test and then a production environment through a repeatable, auditable process rather than by hand. In Fabric terms it means that the content in main is deployed to the Development workspace, then promoted to Test and Production by a deployment pipeline that rebinds environment-specific configuration on the way. The practical effect is a change of posture. Deployment stops being an event performed by the person who happens to know how the workspace is wired, and becomes a process that anyone on the team can run, that produces the same result each time, and that leaves a record. Mechanism one: Git integration Git integration is configured per workspace. Connecting a workspace to a repository branch and folder causes Fabric to serialize the definitions of supported items into that folder as text — JSON for reports and pipelines, .py for notebooks, a model.bim for semantic models, SQL project files for warehouses — and to keep the two in step through explicit Commit and Update actions. What it is responsible for: Version history of item definitions, with the ability to return to any earlier commit. Isolated development through branches, and a branch workspace per branch. Code review through the pull request mechanism of the Git provider. The mirrored folder structure between workspace and repository. What it is explicitly not responsible for: Data. Lakehouse files and tables, warehouse row data and shortcut contents are not version-controlled. A lakehouse is represented in Git by a placeholder that records its existence and name. Workspace configuration. Workspace access roles, capacity assignment and deployment pipeline definitions are managed in the Fabric service and are not part of the repository. Unsupported items. Anything the integration does not support is ignored — not synchronized, but not deleted either. It appears in the source control pane and cannot be committed or updated. Mechanism two: deployment pipelines A deployment pipeline is Fabric's native release-management tool. It provides a small number of ordered stages — conventionally Development, Test and Production — and promotes content from one to the next. Its value is threefold: it gives release managers a controlled path that does not require Git expertise; it produces an auditable record of what was promoted and when; and, through deployment rules, it rebinds environment-specific configuration so that content behaves correctly in each stage. Deployment pipelines are documented separately This playbook stops at the point where main is merged and the Development workspace is updated from Git. Stage configuration, deployment rules and promotion approvals are the subject of a companion release-management document. They are referenced here only where a decision in this playbook constrains them. Mechanism three: the Variable Library A Variable Library is a workspace item containing named variables, each with a set of values — one value set per lifecycle stage, or per developer. Exactly one value set is active in a workspace at a time. title: Prerequisites and tenant configuration
body: Prerequisites and tenant configuration Nothing in this playbook works until a small number of gatekeeping settings are in place on both platforms. They are unremarkable individually; the reason they are treated carefully here is that they are usually owned by different teams, and the integration is frequently blocked by a setting nobody realised they needed to request. Capacity Git integration requires a Fabric capacity. All supported Fabric item types need one; an existing Power BI Premium capacity can be used, but certain Power BI SKUs support Power BI items only. Branch-out also requires available capacity at the moment the operation runs — a branch workspace must be assigned to a capacity to function, and a branch-out will fail if none is available. Plan branch workspace capacity explicitly A team of eight developers each holding an open branch workspace is eight additional workspaces drawing on capacity. Decide up front whether they share the main capacity or use a dedicated development capacity, and set an expectation that branch workspaces are deleted when their release ships. Fabric tenant settings The following tenant switches must be enabled. Depending on the tenant's delegation configuration, they may be set by a tenant administrator, a capacity administrator or a workspace administrator. Required Fabric tenant settings Users can create Fabric items Permits creation of the notebooks, pipelines, lakehouses and models that source control will manage. Users cannot create the assets the integration exists to version. Users can synchronize workspace items with their Git repositories The master switch that activates Git integration across the tenant. The Git integration tab does not function in workspace settings. Users can sync workspace items with GitHub repositories Provider-specific switch for GitHub. Distinct from the general switch above. GitHub cannot be selected as a provider even though Git integration is enabled. Create workspaces Required for branch-out to a new workspace, which is the foundation of the isolated development workflow. Developers cannot branch out to a new workspace. See Section 12.4 for the reconciliation. Service principals can call Fabric public APIs (Developer settings) Required for any CI/CD automation that calls the Fabric REST API. The specific service principal, or a security group containing it, must be added to the allowed list. Automation cannot authenticate. Interactive Git integration is unaffected. Users can export items to Git repositories in other geographical locations Needed when the workspace and repository are in different regions. Applies to Azure DevOps; not required for GitHub. Cross-region export is blocked for Azure DevOps repositories. Users can export workspace items with applied sensitivity labels to Git repositories Only relevant if items carry sensitivity labels and the organization has decided to permit their export. Items with sensitivity labels cannot be committed. See Section 10.2. A permission change is coming From 1 December 2026, users without read-write permission on workspace items cannot use Git integration. Where sensitivity labels or protection policies restrict a user's access to particular items, that user may lose the ability to use Git integration in that workspace. title: Authentication and identity
body: Authentication and identity The most common security mistake in this pattern is to use one identity for everything — typically a long-lived token belonging to whoever set the integration up. The platform pushes you away from that, because the interactive connection and the automation path use different identity types and cannot be collapsed into one. Figure 2 sets out the two tiers and what each is used for. Figure 2. The two tiers. Tier 1 is a person acting interactively; Tier 2 is a workload acting without a person present. Neither can substitute for the other, and the constraint that forces the split is a platform one, not a policy choice. Why the split is unavoidable Fabric documents service principal authentication for the Git connection when the provider is Azure DevOps. For GitHub, the only documented credential for the workspace-to-repository connection is a personal access token, and the platform treats that synchronization as a user-delegated action authenticated by an individual's credentials. Plan on the basis that a non-human identity cannot own a GitHub Git connection, and re-verify before designing around any contrary behaviour you encounter — this is an area the platform has been changing. The consequence is a deliberate two-tier model: Tier 1 — interactive. Developers connect their branch workspaces and perform commits and updates using their own Microsoft Entra ID account and their own fine-grained personal access token. Tier 2 — automated. GitHub Actions and any administrative automation authenticate as an Entra ID service principal whose credentials are held in environment-scoped GitHub secrets, and which is granted access to the target workspaces explicitly. This separation is desirable independently of the platform constraint. A developer's token reaches only the repositories and branches that developer may touch. Automation credentials reach only the environment whose job is running. When someone leaves, revoking their account does not break the pipeline. When a pipeline is compromised, no individual's access is implicated. Authentication strength must match The authentication method in Fabric must be at least as strong as the method required by the Git provider. If GitHub requires multi-factor authentication, Fabric must require it too. Mismatched strength causes connection failures that are not obviously about authentication. Tier 1: creating a fine-grained personal access token GitHub offers classic and fine-grained personal access tokens. Fine-grained tokens are the recommended choice because they can be scoped to a single repository and a minimal permission set, which a classic token cannot. Each person creates their own. Give the token a name that identifies its purpose, for example fabric-<proj>-sync, and set an expiry. Choose the shortest interval the team can operate with; treat anything beyond 90 days as requiring a stated justification. Under Resource owner, select the organization that owns the repository. Depending on organization policy, the token may require approval by an organization owner before it becomes usable. Under Repository access, choose Only select repositories and select the single repository for this project. Do not grant access to all repositories. Under Permissions → Repository permissions, set Contents to Read and write. This is the minimum required for Fabric to read from and write to the repository. body: Repository and workspace topology Naming and structure decisions are cheap to make and expensive to change, because the workspace name, the Git folder name and the branch name are all part of the connection. Settle them before the first workspace is connected. Figure 3 shows the three-way relationship between a workspace, the Git folder it is connected to, and the branch that folder sits on. Figure 3. The three-way mapping. A workspace connects to exactly one branch and one folder. The folder tree inside that folder mirrors the workspace, and is identical across every branch. The medallion layers shown are an illustrative example, not a requirement. The mirrored structure When a workspace is connected and synchronized, its structure — including subfolders — is reproduced inside the connected Git folder. Items in workspace folders are exported to folders of the same name; items in Git folders are imported to folders of the same name. Each item occupies its own folder containing a .platform file and the definition files for that item type. Behaviour worth knowing before designing a structure: Empty folders are not copied to Git. A folder appears in Git when an item is created in it or moved into it. Empty folders in Git are deleted automatically. Empty folders in the workspace are not deleted automatically, even after every item has been moved out. Folder structure is preserved to ten levels of depth. An item whose display name exceeds 256 characters, ends with a period or space, or contains a forbidden character has its Git folder renamed to the item's logical ID and type — which makes the repository considerably harder to read. Naming standards The following conventions are offered as a working default. The specific strings matter less than choosing one scheme and applying it without exception. Recommended naming conventions Workspace <ORG>-FAB-<PROJ>-<LAYER>-<STAGE> ACME-FAB-FIN-BRZ-DEV Sorts predictably in the workspace list. Layer and stage are both explicit, so no workspace is ambiguous. Branch workspace <ORG>-FAB-<PROJ>-FEAT-<nn> ACME-FAB-FIN-FEAT-03 Numbered rather than named after a person, so the workspace outlives an individual's involvement. Repository <proj>-fabric fin-fabric Lower case, hyphenated, within the <org> GitHub organization. Git folder /<LAYER> /BRZ One folder per layer workspace, at the root of the repository. Identical in every branch. Feature branch feature/<topic>_<YYYY_MM> feature/income_statement_2026_03 Purpose is legible; snake_case is tooling-friendly; the date marks the target period. Bug fix branch bugfix/<topic> bugfix/sales_report_filter For corrective work that is not an emergency. Hotfix branch hotfix/<incident-id> hotfix/INC-10482 Ties the branch to the incident record. Reserved for emergency production fixes. Variable Library <PROJ>_config FIN_config One per workspace that needs environment-specific values. Why a date marker in the branch name earns its place feature/income_statement_2026_03 answers three questions at a glance: what the work is, when it was targeted, and whether it is stale. A branch list is one of the few places where redundant information is worth the characters. Repository granularity: the decision to make deliberately The recommendation here is one repository per project, with one folder per layer workspace. Three alternatives are defensible, and the choice depends on how independently the domains in your estate release. Repository granularity trade-offs One repository per project (recommended) Layers within a project release together and are owned by one team. The whole project can be reviewed, branched and reverted as a unit. Cross-project changes require coordinated pull requests in more than one repository. One repository for the estate A single team owns everything and governance is best applied once, centrally. Release cadences become coupled. A pull request touches unrelated domains. body: Connecting a workspace safely This is the section to read before touching source-control settings. Connecting a workspace to a repository is a single dialog with a destructive failure mode, and the destruction is silent, immediate and not reversible. Everything that follows is a procedure designed around that one fact. What actually happens when you connect When a workspace is connected to a branch and folder, Fabric immediately makes the two match. If you then run Update workspace from Git while that folder is empty or near-empty, Fabric resolves the workspace to match — and removes items. A Git branch can always be restored to an earlier commit. A workspace cannot. Figure 4 sets out the decision and both of its outcomes. The procedure in Section 7.3 exists to guarantee you take the left-hand path. Figure 4. The first-sync decision. The left path is safe and is the one this procedure is designed to guarantee you take. The right path is where workspaces are lost. Why the failure mode exists The rule Fabric applies to the first synchronization is reasonable in isolation: if one side is empty and the other has content, copy from the non-empty side to the empty one. If both sides have content, ask the user which direction to take. The problem is what counts as content. A repository prepared in advance — with a README.md, a .gitignore, or placeholder layer folders created helpfully by whoever set it up — is not empty. The first sync therefore presents a choice, and one of the two options is Update workspace with Git content, which overwrites the workspace with a folder containing almost nothing. The dialog does warn, and asks for confirmation. It is nonetheless chosen, under time pressure, by people who reasonably assume that a fresh repository is empty. Do not pre-create folders in the repository Fabric creates the folder structure during synchronization. An 'empty' folder in GitHub containing only a README.md or a .gitkeep will not behave as empty. Create the repository, leave it alone, and let the first commit from the workspace populate it. Preflight: clone the workspace as a rollback target Because a workspace cannot be restored to a previous state, the only meaningful safety net is a second workspace holding a verified copy. A deployment pipeline stage is the most convenient way to produce one. Create or identify a spare target workspace to act as the clone. Use a deployment pipeline to deploy from the source workspace to that target. Fabric copies item definitions into the target. Re-hydrate the data. This step is not optional and is the one most often skipped — see the caution below. Run the clone. Execute the pipelines, refresh the models, open the reports. An unverified backup is not a backup. Record what the clone is for and when it may be deleted, so it is not mistaken for a live environment. A pipeline clone does not copy data For a lakehouse, Fabric creates a new, empty lakehouse in the target: no files, no tables. The SQL analytics endpoint and semantic model objects are provisioned, and notebooks and Spark job definitions are re-bound to the new lakehouse item. Shortcut definitions are synchronized; shortcut contents are not. Warehouse objects are created from the schema project, without row data. A clone is therefore a functional shell until you load data into it. Treat re-hydration and verification as part of the preflight, not as a follow-up task. The workspace administrator performing them should have the repository open in a second window to confirm the folder state before proceeding. Confirm the preflight clone exists, has data, and runs. In GitHub, confirm the target branch exists and that the folder name you intend to use does not exist yet. You will type the folder name during connection; Fabric creates it. title: The synchronization model
body: The synchronization model Commit and Update look symmetrical and are not. Commit is selective and additive; Update is total and overwrites. Most day-to-day confusion about Fabric Git integration traces back to that asymmetry. Figure 5 summarizes the model and the states a workspace reports between the two actions. Figure 5. Commit moves selected items from the workspace to the branch. Update takes the entire branch and applies it to the workspace. The states listed on the right are what the workspace reports between those two actions. Bidirectional, but never simultaneous Synchronization runs in one direction at a time. You cannot commit and update together. If changes have arrived in the branch, commits are disabled until the workspace has been updated. If the same item has been changed in both the workspace and the branch, updates are disabled until the conflict is resolved. Update first, then commit When both directions have pending work: update, resolve any conflict, verify the workspace still behaves, then commit. Attempting to force the sequence the other way produces conflicts that are harder to reason about than the ones you started with. Commit Changed items appear under Changes. Where more than one item has changed, you choose which to commit. A commit message is optional; if omitted, a default is supplied. Supply one anyway — the default tells a reviewer nothing. Commits are disabled while updates are pending. During a commit, Fabric deletes files inside an item folder that are not part of that item's definition. Files elsewhere in the repository, outside item folders, are left alone. Do not store anything of your own inside an item folder. A preview capability allows file-level commits within an item from the compare experience, for supported item types. Update Update always applies the entire branch and syncs to the most recent commit. Individual items cannot be selected — this is the principal asymmetry with commit. Folder changes are applied along with item changes. Items present in the workspace but absent from the branch are removed. Updates are disabled if the same item has changed in both places, until the conflict is resolved. title: Bidirectional, but never simultaneous
body: The synchronization model Commit and Update look symmetrical and are not. Commit is selective and additive; Update is total and overwrites. Most day-to-day confusion about Fabric Git integration traces back to that asymmetry. Figure 5 summarizes the model and the states a workspace reports between the two actions. Figure 5. Commit moves selected items from the workspace to the branch. Update takes the entire branch and applies it to the workspace. The states listed on the right are what the workspace reports between those two actions. Bidirectional, but never simultaneous Synchronization runs in one direction at a time. You cannot commit and update together. If changes have arrived in the branch, commits are disabled until the workspace has been updated. If the same item has been changed in both the workspace and the branch, updates are disabled until the conflict is resolved. Update first, then commit When both directions have pending work: update, resolve any conflict, verify the workspace still behaves, then commit. Attempting to force the sequence the other way produces conflicts that are harder to reason about than the ones you started with. Commit Changed items appear under C

title: Supported items and their representation in Git
body: Supported items and their representation in Git Knowing what the integration covers is a planning input, not a detail. An unsupported item is not protected by any of the controls in this playbook, and its absence from the repository is silent — it simply never appears. Verify this inventory before relying on it Fabric's supported-item list changes frequently and many entries are in preview. The inventory below was accurate when this document was written. Check the current vendor documentation before making a design decision that depends on an item type being supported — particularly for a preview item. How items are represented in Git Supported items are written out as human-readable text, which is what makes review and diffing possible. Each item occupies a folder containing a .platform file plus its definition files. Representation of commonly used items Report A folder containing a .pbir definition and report.json, describing layout, visuals and configuration. Yes, though large visual changes produce noisy diffs. Paginated report A single .rdl file — an XML representation of the report definition. Yes. Semantic model A folder containing definition.pbidataset and model.bim. The .bim is a JSON representation of the Tabular Object Model. Yes. Expect column-order noise (Section 8.6). Notebook A folder containing a .py file plus metadata preserving markdown cells and the attached lakehouse and environment configuration. Cell outputs are not saved. Yes — notebooks diff well, which makes them the easiest item type to review. Lakehouse A placeholder recording the item's existence and name. The data in OneLake is not version-controlled. No meaningful content to review. Spark job definition Definition and configuration saved as source files. Yes. Environment Configuration including library specifications and Spark compute settings, as text. Yes — and valuable, because environment drift is otherwise invisible. Warehouse The full schema — tables, views, stored procedures — as a SQL database project: a set of .sql files organized into folders. Yes. This is the standard format for database source control. Mirrored database Configuration and definition as a .json file. Yes, for settings changes. Data pipeline The pipeline definition — activities, parameters, structure — as a .json file. Yes, with practice. Nested activity JSON is verbose. Variable Library Variables and value sets as JSON, deployable like any other item. Yes — and this is where environment configuration becomes reviewable. Supported item inventory The following item types supported Git integration at the time of writing. title: Exclusions, sensitivity labels and limits
body: Exclusions, sensitivity labels and limits What the integration does not cover is as much a design input as what it does. An unsupported item is protected by none of the controls in this playbook, and its absence from the repository is silent. Unsupported items and exclusions The following are not part of the repository synchronization. Some are item types; others are categories of configuration that live only in the Fabric service. Not covered by Git integration Power BI dashboards Not versioned; changes are unrecoverable through Git. Prefer reports, which are supported. Where a dashboard is required, document its definition outside Fabric. SQL analytics endpoint of a lakehouse The lakehouse item is tracked; its endpoint is not. Nothing to do — the endpoint is derived from the lakehouse. Semantic models: push datasets, live connections to Azure Analysis Services or SQL Server Analysis Services, model v1, streaming datasets These model types cannot be versioned. Migrate to a supported model type where the workload allows it. Reports depending on models in Analysis Services, or exported from Power BI Desktop against a model in My workspace Excluded from report support. Re-point the report at a workspace-hosted semantic model. Workspace access roles Who can do what in a workspace is not in the repository. Manage in the Fabric service, sourced from identity provider groups (Section 15.4). Deployment pipeline definitions The release path itself is not versioned. Document stage configuration and deployment rules in the companion release-management document. Capacity assignment Not in the repository. Manage as platform configuration. All lakehouse and warehouse data Definitions are versioned; rows, files and tables are not. Data protection is a separate discipline. Git integration is not a backup. Items with sensitivity labels Export may be disabled, so these items cannot be committed. An administrator can enable export of labelled items. Decide this deliberately — it is a data-protection decision, not a tooling one. Git submodules Not supported. Restructure to avoid them. Workspaces with template apps installed Cannot be connected to Git at all. Separate template app content into its own workspace. My workspace Cannot connect to a Git provider. Develop in a proper workspace, never in My workspace. Sovereign clouds Not supported. — B2B guest scenarios Not supported for sync and commit. Provision internal accounts for contributors who need to commit. Sensitivity labels and data protection Items carrying sensitivity labels are not supported by default, and their export may be disabled — which means they cannot be committed. An administrator can enable the tenant setting that permits export of labelled items to Git repositories, with the label removed. This is a data-protection decision rather than a tooling one, and it should be made by whoever owns information protection, not by whoever is configuring source control. The question to answer is whether the repository is an appropriate location for the content the label was applied to protect. The repository typically has a different access list from the workspace, is readable by everyone with repository Read, and retains history indefinitely. Decide this explicitly, and record who decided Either labelled items are excluded from source control — accepting that they are unversioned — or export is enabled and the repository is brought within the scope of the relevant data-protection controls. Both are defensible. Leaving it undecided means the behaviour is determined by a tenant default. Git integration is not a backup It versions definitions. It does not version data. A workspace restored entirely from Git is a functional shell with no rows in it. Data protection requires its own strategy, and that strategy is out of scope here — but its absence is not. title: The branching model
body: The branching model GitHub Flow has one long-lived branch and a rule about how changes reach it. Its simplicity is the point: the protection comes from the review gate, not from branch topology, so adding branches adds process without adding safety. The three principles The three principles of GitHub Flow main is always deployable The content of main is production-ready at all times. Anything merged into it should be safe to deploy immediately. This is why main is what the Development workspaces are connected to, and why the ruleset in Section 16 exists. All work happens on short-lived branches Every change — new feature, enhancement, bug fix — begins with a branch created from the current main. The branch is scoped to one unit of work and is deleted when it merges. 'Short-lived' means days, not months. Changes return only through a pull request The pull request is where review, discussion and automated checks happen. There is no other path into main, and the repository enforces that rather than relying on people to remember. Why not GitFlow GitFlow maintains main, develop, release and hotfix branches simultaneously. It was designed for software shipped in versioned releases to customers who cannot upgrade on demand. Analytics platforms are rarely in that position: content is promoted to a small number of environments the team controls, and the cadence is iterative. Applied to Fabric, GitFlow's additional branches mostly create additional workspaces to keep in step. Each long-lived branch wants a workspace connected to it, each workspace consumes capacity, and each pair is another thing that can drift. The review gate — which is what actually prevents bad changes reaching production — is identical in both models. Where a long-lived branch does earn its place A release/<version> branch is worth introducing if you genuinely need to maintain a prior version while developing the next — for example a regulatory reporting solution where a filed period must remain reproducible. That is a specific, justified exception, not a default. Figure 6 traces one change through the whole model: three actors, eight steps and one protected branch. Figure 6. One change, end to end. Steps 1 to 3 are the developer in an isolated branch workspace; steps 4 to 7 are the repository and the reviewer; step 8 returns the merged change to the Development workspace and hands it to the release path. Branch naming The convention recommended in Section 6.2 is repeated here because it is the part of this section people look up: Branch naming patterns, with an example of each. The rationale for each element: the prefix groups branches in the branch list and allows a ruleset to target them; the snake_case topic is legible and safe in tooling; the date marker makes a stale branch obvious without opening it. Review the branch list monthly Branches whose date marker has passed and which have not merged are either abandoned or blocked. Both are worth knowing about. A branch list nobody prunes stops being useful within a quarter. Creating a branch A branch can be created in GitHub or from within Fabric. Creating it from within Fabric — through Branch out — is preferred because it creates the branch and the workspace together and connects them, which is the state you actually want. Section 12 covers that path. To create a branch in GitHub directly: Open the repository and select the branch dropdown to review the existing branches. Check whether the work already has a branch before creating another. Select the branch count or the Branches link to open the branches page. Choose New branch. Enter the name following the convention above, and set the source to main. Create the branch. It is now selectable from the dropdown. Always branch from current main Branching from another feature branch couples two units of work: the second cannot merge until the first does, and reverting the first becomes complicated. title: Branch workspaces and isolated development
body: Branch workspaces and isolated development A branch workspace is the feature that makes this model practical in Fabric. It gives each unit of work its own live environment, which is the only way to test a change to a pipeline or a notebook without affecting anyone else. It also has one significant gap, which is the subject of the next section. What branch-out does Branch out is a single operation that performs several actions. From the source workspace's connected branch, Fabric: Creates a new Git branch from the last commit of the source workspace's branch. Creates a new workspace, or repoints an existing one, and connects it to that new branch. Populates the workspace with the item definitions from the branch — all of them by default. Establishes a recorded relationship between the branch workspace and its source workspace. The developer is taken to the new workspace, which is then an isolated environment for that unit of work. The relationship is visible in the Fabric interface in three places: the workspace tree shows the source workspace as the parent; breadcrumbs allow navigation back to it; and the Related branches section of the Branches tab in the source control pane lists linked workspaces so they can be reached from the context of the current work rather than hunted for in a workspace list. The branch-out procedure In the source workspace, open Source control and select Branch out. Choose whether to create a new workspace or branch out into an existing one. Enter the new branch and workspace names, or select the existing workspace. If a branch workspace admin profile is configured, decide whether to use it (Section 12.4). Optionally select Select items individually to include only a subset of items — see Section 12.3. Select Branch out. Fabric validates that your identity can complete the operation before starting, and reports an error rather than beginning an operation that would fail. Wait for the sync to complete; it may take a few minutes. Confirm you are in the new workspace and that the expected items are present. Establish data isolation before making changes — see Section 13. Branching out to an existing workspace can lose work Items in the target workspace that have not been saved to Git may be deleted. title: What branch-out does
body: Branch workspaces and isolated development A branch workspace is the feature that makes this model practical in Fabric. It gives each unit of work its own live environment, which is the only way to test a change to a pipeline or a notebook without affecting anyone else. It also has one significant gap, which is the subject of the next section. What branch-out does Branch out is a single operation that performs several actions. From the source workspace's connected branch, Fabric: Creates a new Git branch from the last commit of the source workspace's branch. Creates a new workspace, or repoints an existing one, and connects it to that new branch. Populates the workspace with the item definitions from the branch — all of them by default. Establishes a recorded relationship between the branch workspace and its source workspace. The developer is taken to the new workspace, which is then an isolated environment for that unit of work. The relationship is visible in the Fabric interface in three places: the workspace tree shows the source workspace as the parent; breadcrumbs allow navigation back to it; and the Related branches section of the Branches tab in the source control pane lists

title: The data isolation problem
body: The data isolation problem This is the most important section in the playbook after Section 7. A branch workspace isolates code. It does not isolate data. Teams that do not address this get the appearance of isolation with none of the substance, and discover the difference when someone truncates a shared table. Data is not copied to a branch workspace Branch-out copies item definitions. A notebook in the new workspace that references a lakehouse will, by default, still connect to the lakehouse in the workspace it was branched from. The same is true of pipelines, dataflows and shortcuts. Figure 7 contrasts the default behaviour with the same two developers once a Variable Library is in place. Figure 7. Left: the default. Two developers in separate branch workspaces, writing to the same physical data. Right: the same two developers with a Variable Library selecting a different data source per value set. The two consequences Consequences of the data isolation gap No real isolation A developer testing a transformation reads from, and writes to, the shared Development lakehouse. A TRUNCATE or an incorrect merge corrupts data that another developer is depending on. The branch workspace provided no protection at all, while advertising that it did. Unreliable tests A test in a branch workspace depends on the state of data in a different workspace. It passes because someone else happened to have loaded the right rows, or fails for reasons unconnected to the change under test. Neither outcome tells you anything, and the team learns to distrust the tests. Option one: parameterization through a Variable Library This is the recommended approach and, since the Variable Library became available, the straightforward one. Design every item to be environment-aware: no hard-coded workspace names, lakehouse references, connection strings or database names. Each environment-specific value is a variable in a Variable Library, and each workspace has an active value set that supplies its own values. Structure: A Variable Library item lives in the workspace and holds named variables. Variables may be basic types — string, integer, boolean — or complex types such as an item reference, which points at a specific lakehouse or warehouse. Each variable has one value per value set. A value set corresponds to a stage (dev, test, prod) or to an individual developer's sandbox. Exactly one value set is active in a workspace at a time, and it determines the values used at runtime. Items resolve values from the active set in their own context — resolution is not tied to deployment. Items that can consume a Variable Library include data pipelines, lakehouse shortcuts, notebooks (through NotebookUtils and the %%configure magic command), Dataflow Gen2, Copy Job, user data functions and Plan items. The second benefit is centralization. If several lakehouses in a workspace use shortcuts to the same source, that source becomes one variable. Changing it is one edit rather than one edit per lakehouse. Variable Library constraints Variables per library Up to 1,000 Value sets per library Up to 1,000 Combined cells in alternative value sets Fewer than 10,000 Item size Must not exceed 1 MB Note and description fields Up to 2,048 characters Value set ordering Value sets appear in the order added and cannot be reordered in the interface. Edit the JSON directly to change the order. Naming Must not be empty, must not have leading or trailing spaces, must start with a letter, may contain letters, numbers, underscores, hyphens and spaces, and must not exceed 256 characters. Names are not case sensitive. Uniqueness Value set names must be unique within a library; variable names must be unique within a library. The same variable name may exist in two different libraries in one workspace. Active value set Always exactly one. An active value set cannot be deleted — activate another first. title: The pull request process
body: The pull request process The pull request is where the quality of this whole model is actually determined. Everything else — branching, rulesets, environments — exists to make sure changes arrive here and cannot go around it. What a pull request is for Three things at once, and it is worth being explicit about all three because teams tend to optimize for the first and neglect the others: A quality gate. A second person looks at the change before it reaches a deployable trunk. A collaboration forum. Reviewers comment on specific lines, ask questions, and suggest improvements. This is the mechanism by which knowledge moves around a team and by which newer engineers learn the codebase. A durable record. Six months later, the pull request is the answer to “why is this measure calculated this way?” — provided the description said something. Opening a pull request Confirm the work is complete and committed to the feature branch, and that unit testing in the branch workspace has passed. In the repository, open the Pull requests tab. Select New pull request, or use Compare & pull request on the banner that appears after a recent push. Set the base branch to main and the compare branch to your feature branch. Review the Comparing changes section: check the commits, the files changed, and the additions and deletions. Read your own diff before asking anyone else to. Enter a title that describes the change, not the branch. Write the description — see the template below. Select Create pull request. What the description should contain A reviewer arriving at a Fabric pull request is looking at JSON they cannot execute. What they need from the author is context they cannot get from the diff. A pull request description template. Consider committing this as .github/pull_request_template.md so it is pre-filled. Reviewing Guidance for reviewers, in rough order of value: Read the description first. If it does not say what the change is for or how it was tested, ask for that before reviewing the code. This is not pedantry — a reviewer who cannot tell what the change is intended to do cannot tell whether it does it. Check the parameterization. Search the diff for hard-coded workspace names, lakehouse references, connection strings and database names. This is the single most productive thing a reviewer can look for in a Fabric change (Section 13.3). Check the blast radius claim. Does the change touch a semantic model that reports depend on? Does a pipeline schedule change? Is a column removed that something downstream reads? Ignore known noise. Column reordering in a .bim after a rename, and LF/CRLF conversion, are artefacts. Do not raise them. Comment on lines, not in a summary. Line comments create a thread that can be resolved; a summary comment listing six issues cannot be tracked. Approve, or request changes, explicitly. A review left in an ambiguous state blocks the author without telling them what to do. To approve: open the pull request, select Files changed or the review control, choose Approve, add comments if useful, and Submit review. A reviewer must hold write access or above for the approval to count. What the author will see while a review is required With the ruleset from Section 16 in place, the pull request shows Review required and Merging is blocked until an approving review from a user with write access has been submitted. This is expected and is the control working. Merging Confirm the required approvals are present and every required status check has passed. Review the commit message and extended description that will be recorded on main. Select Merge pull request, then Confirm merge. Delete the feature branch when prompted. The branch has served its purpose and leaving it makes the branch list less useful. Update the Development workspace from Git — Section 14.6. title: Access model: teams, roles and identity
body: Access model: teams, roles and identity Least privilege is usually stated as a principle and implemented as an exception list. The way to make it hold is structural: grant permissions to a small number of teams whose membership comes from the identity provider, and never to individuals. Figure 8 shows how identity, teams, repository roles and the gates they enforce relate to one another, and where the separate Fabric plane has to be kept aligned. Figure 8. Identity flows from the provider into teams, teams carry repository roles, and the roles determine what the gates permit. The Fabric-side roles are a separate plane that must be kept aligned with the same groups. Least privilege in this context Applied to a Fabric project, least privilege means moving away from the common state in which every developer holds administrative access to the repository. Access is tailored to the distinct functions in a data team: Data engineers and developers need to write code and contribute changes on feature branches. Lead developers and architects need to review and approve changes, and merge them into main. Platform administrators and DevOps engineers need to configure repository settings, manage security and set up automation. Auditors, compliance officers, project managers and business analysts need to see the code and track progress, and nothing more. The reason to bother is not theoretical. The commonest cause of an unreviewed change reaching production is not malice — it is someone with admin rights merging their own pull request at the end of a long day because they could. The team structure Recommended team structure and repository permissions <org>/fabric-admins Admin Owns the health and configuration of the repository: settings, rulesets, environments, secrets and team access. Highly privileged — restrict to a small number of platform owners or DevOps leads, and review the membership as a named control. <org>/fabric-reviewers Maintain Senior developers, technical leads and architects. Acts as the gatekeeper for main: reviews, approves and merges pull requests. Maintain grants those capabilities without access to sensitive repository settings, which is precisely the separation wanted. <org>/fabric-developers Write The primary group: data engineers and analysts actively building Fabric assets. Write permits creating and pushing to feature branches and opening pull requests, and — critically — does not permit merging directly to main or altering protection rules. <org>/fabric-auditors Read Stakeholders who need visibility without any ability to change: compliance officers, project managers, business analysts. Read grants view-only access to code, issues and pull requests. Repository role reference GitHub repository roles Read View and discuss the project. Auditors and observers. Triage Manage issues and pull requests without write access. Support or coordination functions that route work but do not write code. Write Push to the repository and manage their own pull requests. Developers. Maintain All Write capabilities, plus managing some repository settings such as topics and merge configuration. Can act as a designated reviewer and merge approved pull requests. Reviewers and tech leads. Admin Full control, including managing access, changing settings and deleting the repository. Platform owners only. To assign these, a repository administrator opens Settings → Collaborators and teams, invites each team, and selects its role. Grant roles to the teams, not to the people in them. No individual collaborators Every entry in Collaborators and teams should be a team. An individual added directly is invisible to the identity provider, survives the person changing role, and is found during an audit rather than during onboarding. title: Hardening the repository with rulesets
body: Hardening the repository with rulesets A protected branch is the difference between a policy and a control. Everything in Sections 11 to 15 describes how the team should work; this section is where the repository stops relying on them remembering. Rulesets rather than legacy branch protection Branch protection was historically configured through branch protection rules. Rulesets are the modern successor and are what this playbook uses. The differences are material: Rulesets compared with legacy branch protection rules Layering Multiple rulesets can apply to the same branch at once. GitHub aggregates them and applies the most restrictive version of any overlapping rule. Only one rule applies at a time, creating ambiguity when several target the same branch. Visibility Anyone with read access can view the active rulesets, so a developer can see why an action is blocked without needing admin rights. Visible only to administrators, which turns every blocked push into a support question. Manageability Have a status and can be enabled or disabled without being deleted — useful for a planned, audited exception. Must be deleted and recreated. Scope Can be defined at organization level and applied across many repositories, giving consistent governance for an estate. Repository-scoped only. Rule catalogue Broader, including file path, path length, file extension and file size restrictions — several of which map directly onto Fabric's own limits. Narrower. The main branch ruleset Create it from Settings → Rules → Rulesets → New ruleset → New branch ruleset. Give it a name that says what it does, for example main branch protection. Set Enforcement status to Active — a ruleset in evaluate mode reports but does not block. Under Target branches, add a target by pattern and enter main, or use the Default branch inclusion so the ruleset follows the default branch if it is ever renamed. Recommended configuration for main Recommended main ruleset configuration Target main (or Default branch) Targets the deployable trunk. Restrict deletions Enabled Prevents the branch being deleted. On by default. Block force pushes Enabled Protects the integrity of the commit history. Without this, history can be rewritten and the audit trail is worthless. On by default. Two approvals is a meaningful step up in assurance and a meaningful step up in cycle time — choose deliberately. Check names come from the job names in the workflow files. title: Environments and credential management
body: Environments and credential management Storing a production credential as a repository secret makes it readable by a workflow running on any branch, including a developer's experimental one. Environment secrets exist to prevent exactly that, and the difference is the single most consequential choice in this section. The three secret scopes GitHub secret scopes compared Repository All workflows on all branches in one repository. Non-sensitive, general-purpose values used identically everywhere — for example a monitoring tool's non-privileged API key. Avoid for deployment credentials. A workflow on a feature branch can read them, which violates least privilege. Environment Only workflow jobs that explicitly target the named environment, and only after that environment's protection rules are satisfied. Deployment credentials, per environment. Recommended. This is the scope that enforces least privilege for credentials. Organization Selected repositories across the organization. Values genuinely shared by many projects — for example a licence key for an organization-wide tool. Not appropriate unless you are managing many identical Fabric repositories that legitimately share one identity — which is itself worth questioning. Deployment credentials belong to an environment A repository secret is readable by any workflow in the repository, on any branch. That includes a workflow a developer just wrote on a feature branch. Production credentials stored at repository scope are effectively available to anyone who can push a branch. Creating an environment In the repository, go to Settings → Environments → New environment. Name it for the Fabric stage it corresponds to — development, test, production. Start with only the environments you actually deploy to; adding one later is trivial. Select Configure to set its protection rules. Add required reviewers (up to the platform limit) — the people who must approve a deployment to this environment. For production these should be a named, small group. Enable Prevent self-review so the person who triggered a deployment cannot approve it. Consider a wait timer for production, giving a short window in which an unintended deployment can be cancelled. Restrict deployment branches to main only for test and production. This is important: without it, a workflow on any branch can target the environment and read its secrets. Decide on Allow administrators to bypass configured protection rules. Enabling it provides a controlled break-glass path for incidents; it also weakens the control. If you enable it, expect every use to be accompanied by an incident record. Save the protection rules. Check your plan before designing around protection rules On GitHub Free, Pro and Team, deployment protection rules such as required reviewers and wait timers are available for public repositories only. A private Fabric repository needs a GitHub Enterprise plan for those rules. Environment secrets still scope correctly without them, but the approval gate does not exist — so verify this before relying on a reviewer step in your design. Restrict deployment branches, or the environment scope achieves nothing Environment secrets are protected by the environment's rules. If any branch may deploy to that environment, then any branch can obtain its secrets and the distinction from a repository secret has been lost. Limiting deployment branches to main is what makes the scope meaningful. Storing the service principal credentials Go to Settings → Environments and select the environment to configure. Scroll to Environment secrets and select Add secret. Create AZURE_TENANT_ID and paste the Directory (tenant) ID. Create AZURE_CLIENT_ID and paste the Application (client) ID. Create AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET and paste the client secret value. Confirm all three appear under the environment, and that none of them appears under Repository secrets. Repeat for each environment, using a different service principal per environment wherever possible.

title: Optional: automated security scanning
body: Optional: automated security scanning The manual gates in Sections 16 and 17 deliver most of the available risk reduction. This section is a worthwhile second phase, not a prerequisite — with one exception, noted below, which is worth enabling on day one. Secret scanning and push protection Of everything in this section, this is the one to enable immediately. A Fabric repository contains connection definitions, and the failure mode is a credential committed in a pipeline or notebook definition. Push protection rejects the push before the secret reaches the repository at all, which is qualitatively better than detecting it afterwards — a secret that has been pushed must be treated as compromised and rotated, even after the commit is removed. Enable secret scanning and push protection in Settings → Advanced Security. Add the Require secret scanning alerts are resolved rule to the feature branch ruleset so an unresolved alert blocks the merge. Agree the response procedure in advance: rotate the credential first, then remove it from history. The order matters. Licensing Secret scanning and push protection are free for public repositories. For private and internal repositories they require a purchased GitHub Secret Protection licence, which in turn requires a Team or Enterprise plan. If that is not available, the compensating control is a pattern-matching step in the CI checks of Section 18.4 — weaker, but not nothing. A pushed secret is a compromised secret Rewriting history does not undo exposure. Rotate the credential, then clean the repository. Never the other way round, and never only the second. Code scanning CodeQL analyses code for vulnerability patterns. Its value in a Fabric repository is narrower than in an application repository, because most of what is committed is JSON definitions rather than executable code. The useful target is the Python in notebooks and Spark job definitions. Enable code scanning and configure CodeQL for Python. Add Require code scanning results to the main ruleset, with a severity threshold you are prepared to enforce. Expect to tune it. Notebook code triggers patterns that are not meaningful in a data engineering context, and an unusable alert list gets ignored wholesale. Dependency scanning Dependabot monitors declared dependencies for known vulnerabilities and opens pull requests to update them. In a Fabric repository the relevant surface is the library specifications in Environment items and any requirements files committed alongside notebooks. Environment items are where dependencies actually live Fabric Environment items carry library specifications and are Git-supported. That makes them reviewable — a genuine gain, because environment drift is otherwise invisible — but the format may not be one Dependabot understands. Review environment changes manually in the pull request regardless of what automated tooling reports. Continuous integration checks Where the team is prepared to invest, automated verification on each pull request is the highest-value addition to this framework. title: Rollback and restore
body: Rollback and restore The question that determines the method is not which command is cleaner. It is whether anyone else has pulled the commit. Get that wrong and a recovery becomes a second incident. Figure 9 sets out the decision, both procedures, and the Fabric re-sync that must follow either of them. Figure 9. The decision, both procedures, and the Fabric re-sync that has to follow either of them. Choosing the method Rollback method selection The commits are on a shared branch — main, or a feature branch a colleague has pulled. git revert Non-destructive. Creates a new commit that inverts the change, preserving history. Safe for any branch other people use. The commits are only on your machine, or on a private branch nobody else has pulled. git reset --hard Rewrites history by moving the branch pointer. Faster and cleaner, and unsafe anywhere shared. The change is in the workspace but has not been committed. Fabric Undo The source control pane can discard uncommitted workspace changes. Use this before reaching for Git at all. The workspace has been emptied by a bad sync. See Section 7.5 This is a different problem — the branch is intact and the workspace is not. Never reset --hard a shared branch Rewriting the history of a branch others have pulled leaves their local copies inconsistent with the remote. The next person to pull gets a confusing divergence, and someone will resolve it by force-pushing their own stale version back. If the commit has been shared, revert it. Method one: git revert The safe method, and the one to use for anything that has reached main. Scenario: a merged change has introduced a defect and must be undone without disrupting anyone else's history. Prepare the local repository Identify the commit Identify the hash of the commit to undo. Here it is d7f3346. Revert Git opens your editor to confirm the commit message for the new revert commit. The default — Revert "add currency conversion to revenue measure" — is usually adequate; add the incident reference if there is one. Save and close to finalize. To revert a range, revert newest-first to avoid conflicts, or specify the range directly: Reverting a merge commit needs -m 1 to indicate which parent to treat as the mainline. title: Auditing, monitoring and scaling
body: Auditing, monitoring and scaling The framework produces evidence as a by-product. Whether that evidence is ever looked at is a separate decision, and it is the difference between a governed environment and one that merely looks governed. What each platform records Available audit evidence GitHub audit log Repository setting changes, team membership changes, ruleset creation and modification, bypass events, secret creation, environment changes. Ruleset weakening; bypass events; individuals added directly as collaborators; secrets added at repository scope. GitHub pull request history Every change, its author, its reviewers, its approvals, its checks, its discussion. Changes merged without the expected approval; approvals dismissed then re-granted quickly; a pattern of self-approval. Fabric activity log Workspace and item operations, including Git integration actions and API calls by the service principal. Commits and updates outside expected hours; connections established outside the documented procedure; service principal activity from unexpected sources. Fabric monitoring hub Pipeline and notebook execution history and outcomes. Failures after a deployment; execution in workspaces that should be dormant. Deployment pipeline history What was promoted, by whom, when. Promotions not traceable to a merged pull request. A review cadence that is actually followed A comprehensive review nobody performs is worth less than a short one somebody does. The following is intended to be sustainable. Suggested review cadence Weekly Stale branches and branch workspaces. Anything whose date marker has passed and which has not merged. 10 minutes Monthly Bypass events in the audit log. Pull requests merged with fewer approvals than the ruleset requires. Any ruleset change. 30 minutes Quarterly Team membership against the identity provider. Repository collaborators — confirm every entry is still a team. Service principal API permissions and workspace roles. Personal access token expiries. The branch workspace admin profile's consented identity. 2 hours Quarterly Re-run the ruleset verification tests from Section 16.8 and retain the evidence. 1 hour Annually, or on change This playbook, against current platform behaviour. Preview capabilities in particular. 1 day Scaling beyond one project The pattern described here is per project. Applying it to a dozen projects by repeating the configuration twelve times guarantees twelve variations. Four mechanisms prevent that: Organization-level rulesets. Define the main protection once at organization level and apply it to every repository matching a naming pattern. New repositories inherit the protection rather than needing it applied. Organization-level rulesets are available on GitHub Team and Enterprise plans; enterprise-level rulesets are Enterprise-only. Organization-level secrets, for the genuinely shared values only. Resist the temptation to centralize deployment credentials — see Section 17.1. Reusable workflows. Define the deployment and verification workflows once in a shared repository and call them from each project, so a change to the deployment pattern is made in one place. A repository template. A template repository carrying the CODEOWNERS file, the pull request template, the workflow definitions and the documentation stub means every new project starts correctly configured rather than being corrected later. The template is the highest-leverage item Most drift between projects originates in the first hour of a repository's life, when someone configures it from memory. A template removes that hour. Advanced testing Where the team is ready to go further than Section 18.4: Unit-test notebook logic. Extract transformations into functions and test them with a standard framework. The constraint is usually notebook structure, not tooling — logic embedded in cells that assume a live lakehouse cannot be tested in isolation. Data quality expectations. title: Implementation roadmap
body: Implementation roadmap Sequencing matters here more than usual, because two of these phases are safety nets for the ones that follow. Phase 0 exists so that Phase 1 cannot lose anything; Phase 2 exists so that Phase 3's isolation is real rather than nominal. Phased implementation 0 · Prepare Nothing can be lost. Confirm tenant settings and capacity. Create the GitHub organization, teams and repository. Resolve all placeholders and record the decisions. Clone each workspace as a rollback target, re-hydrate its data and verify it runs. Issue fine-grained PATs. Every workspace has a verified clone. The repository exists and is empty. Every placeholder is resolved. 1 · Connect Source control in place, non-destructively. Connect each layer workspace to main and its own folder, following Section 7.3 exactly. Commit a baseline immediately. Verify the repository structure mirrors each workspace. Every workspace is connected and synced. A baseline commit exists on main. A round trip — commit then update — has succeeded. 2 · Parameterize Environment values are externalized. Create a Variable Library per workspace. Replace every hard-coded workspace name, lakehouse reference, connection string and database name. Define a value set per stage. Commit and verify each item still resolves correctly. No item contains a hard-coded environment value. Each stage has a value set. Items run correctly with the stage's set active. 3 · Branch Isolated development works. Establish the branch naming convention. Configure a branch workspace admin profile if workspace creation is centralized. Perform a pilot branch-out, develop a real change in it, and take it through a pull request. Add per-developer value sets or seeding. A developer can branch out, build, test against isolated data, and merge without administrative assistance. 4 · Harden The controls are enforced, not documented. Create the teams and assign repository roles. Add CODEOWNERS. Configure the main and feature branch rulesets. Run the verification tests in Section 16.8 and retain the evidence. Enable secret scanning and push protection. Every verification test in Section 16.8 fails as expected. Evidence retained. 5 · Automate credentials Automation has its own identity. Create the service principal. Enable the tenant setting and grant workspace access. Create the environments with protection rules and restricted deployment branches. Store credentials as environment secrets. Document the rotation policy. No deployment credential exists at repository scope. A test deployment authenticates as the service principal. 6 · Extend Continuous verification. Add CI checks in the order given in Section 18.4, starting with the hard-coded-value scan. Promote each to a required status check once stable. Establish the review cadence. Build the repository template. Required status checks pass consistently. The review cadence has run at least twice. Do not reorder phases 0 to 2 Phase 0 is the safety net for Phase 1's destructive potential. Phase 2 is what makes Phase 3's isolation real. A team that goes straight to branch-out has developers working in workspaces that write to shared data, which is worse than not having branch workspaces at all — because everyone believes they are isolated. Sequence, do not schedule, in this document Durations depend on estate size, item count, how much hard-coding exists and how quickly administrative requests are served. Record your own dates in Appendix G. The dependency order above is the part that transfers between organizations.

title: Strategic recommendations
body: Strategic recommendations A summary of the judgements embedded in this playbook, separated from the procedures, so they can be argued with directly. The unified view The framework as a whole is a single gated flow: Foundation. The tenant and repository are configured and connected. A two-tier authentication model is established: developers hold fine-grained personal access tokens for interactive work; automation uses a service principal whose credentials are environment-scoped. Development. A developer creates a short-lived feature branch and branches out to an isolated workspace. Data sources resolve through a Variable Library, so the isolation is real. Integration. A pull request carries the change back to main. It is the point at which quality is determined: peer review by the reviewers team, plus whatever automated checks exist, enforced by a ruleset rather than by convention. Release. main updates the Development workspaces, and deployment pipelines promote through protected environments to production. Every production change is therefore versioned, peer-reviewed, scanned, traceable to a person and a discussion, and reversible. That combination is the deliverable — not the tooling. Ten recommendations Ten recommendations 1 Treat the first synchronization as a change-controlled event. A clone, a second pair of eyes on the folder state, and a baseline commit within minutes. This is the only irreversible step in the whole process. 2 Externalize every environment-specific value before enabling branch-out. Section 13 is load-bearing. Without it, branch workspaces provide the appearance of isolation and none of the substance, which is a worse position than having no branch workspaces at all. 3 Use a branch workspace admin profile if workspace creation is centralized. It resolves the tension between self-service development and central control, and it is the most valuable capability added to this pattern since it was first written. Assign the consented identity deliberately — it is a single point of failure. 4 Grant repository permissions to teams sourced from the identity provider, never to individuals. The leaver gap is the most common genuine security finding in this area, and SCIM closes it without anyone having to remember. 5 Put deployment credentials in environment secrets and restrict deployment branches. Repository secrets are readable by any workflow on any branch. Restricting deployment branches to main is what makes the environment scope meaningful rather than decorative. 6 Enable secret scanning with push protection on day one. Of everything optional, this is the one to do immediately. Rejecting a secret before it is pushed is qualitatively better than detecting it afterwards, because a pushed secret must be rotated regardless. 7 Enforce Fabric's own limits in the repository. File size, path length and path restriction rules turn silent sync failures into clear push rejections that name the problem. 8 Verify the controls and keep the evidence. Run the tests in Section 16.8. An untested control is an assumption, and the evidence is far easier to capture now than to reconstruct during an audit. 9 Treat bypass as an audited exception. Grant it to a small named group, expect an incident record with each use, and review bypass events on a schedule rather than on suspicion. This is the mechanism by which a control quietly stops being one. 10 Re-verify this playbook against the platform at least quarterly. Several capabilities described here were in preview. Fabric Git integration changes faster than most documentation cycles, and a playbook describing behaviour the platform no longer has is worse than none. The trade-offs worth stating plainly Acknowledged trade-offs Branch workspaces consume capacity. Real, and the cost is proportional to team size and branch discipline.
